content: The symptoms primarily involve skin irritations, which can be either itchy or painful. These skin manifestations are sometimes mistaken for hives. In most cases, PLE resolves on its own without requiring medical intervention, and the skin lesions generally do not leave any scars. The incidence of PLE is most prevalent during the months between spring and autumn in the northern hemisphere. It is estimated that approximately 10-20% of the population is affected by this condition. Women are more frequently affected than men, and PLE can occur across all ethnic groups. Research indicates that around 20% of individuals with PLE have a family history of the condition. Most individuals who develop PLE experience their first episode before the age of 30. The exact cause of PLE remains unknown, but it is hypothesized to involve a type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. Diagnosis: Physical Examination of the Skin The diagnosis of PLE is primarily clinical and involves a thorough physical examination of the skin. Visual inspection of the affected areas often reveals characteristic skin changes associated with PLE. These findings are documented in dermatological resources, such as the Dermatology Atlas, which provides detailed visual references for the condition. Experimental Treatments As of 2008, an Australian company named Clinuvel Pharmaceuticals Limited has been conducting clinical trials to explore the use of a melanocyte-stimulating hormone called melanotan (referred to as CUV1647) as a potential treatment for polymorphous light eruption.
